source.title: Next-token pretraining implies in-context learning
source.authors: P. Riechers; Henry R. Bigelow; Eric A. Alt; A. Shai

record.tranche_reason: It tests in-context loss dynamics on synthetic sequence data and reports training-loss transitions, but does not reproduce the original induction-head identification or circuit analysis.
record.gate_note: The study discusses induction heads and reports a toy Wonka–Dursley example with an induction-like name-prediction behavior and a loss bump. It does not directly identify heads, test previous-token-head composition, or intervene on induction heads. Other results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Only the Wonka–Dursley experiment bears on the claim. A small 2-layer transformer with MLPs shows a loss bump over training, which the authors tie to the induction-head phase change, plus induction-like name copying. A GRU RNN, which cannot implement induction heads, shows the same bump signature. Heads are never identified, and their formation timing is not measured. The synthetic-process experiments measure in-context loss profiles against data structure, not induction heads.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors argue that in-distribution ICL is a mathematically inevitable consequence of next-token loss minimisation, and that the data's structure (especially non-ergodicity) precisely predicts in-context loss dynamics. They report verifying this in toy transformers, reproducing a loss-bump phase transition and power-law in-context loss. They add that performance on one task is coupled to the pretraining task ensemble. They frame induction heads as useful for disambiguating ergodic components, but do not measure them.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains synthetic-data transformers and an RNN and measures in-context loss by position and training progress. It does not use the original induction-head circuit identification or intervention method.
record.method_sensitivity: The in-context loss profile changes with the synthetic process's correlational structure and, for biased-coin data, with the number and distribution of ergodic components. Transformer and RNN training curves differ, although their final in-context loss profiles are reported as similar.

fits_no_version.finding: In small transformers, the shape of in-context loss against token position is set by the data's correlational structure, and it matches theoretical myopic entropy curves. The study reports no ICL for IID data, a one-step drop for Markov data, exponential decay for the Even process, and power laws for non-ergodic many-coin data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The in-context loss profile of a well-trained next-token predictor is determined by the training data's correlational structure, independent of the mechanism.

fits_no_version.finding: A GRU RNN reaches nearly the same final in-context loss profile as the transformer on the Wonka–Dursley process, without induction heads.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-distribution copying-style in-context loss reduction can be achieved by non-induction-head mechanisms.

record.problems: The induction-head mechanism is not directly measured or intervened on. The Wonka–Dursley findings are presented as plots without numerical values in the text, and the reported phase-transition signature does not establish exact coincidence, a narrow early-training window, or head formation. Experiments use synthetic processes and small models; no large-transformer test of the role of induction heads is reported.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Figure-only values are recorded as figure only; descriptions in the text are included where available.

untested.parts: No identification of heads, no previous-token-head composition, and no attention-only model. Only behavioural name copying is shown (r3).
Induction-head formation is never measured. Abruptness, the narrow early window, and timing coincidence with the ICL gain are not quantified.
No large models and no attribution of in-context learning to heads.
No survey of induction heads across models, sizes or runs.
No measurement of whether or when induction heads form under different data. ICL persistence over training is not studied.
Few-shot task learning is not distinguished from copying.
The structure of formation into sub-steps is not analysed.

record.verdict_notes: The reader over-linked V5. That version concerns induction-head formation and ICL persistence, while rows r6–r15 only show data-dependent in-context loss profiles, so I moved them to fits_no_version. The Wonka–Dursley transformer is 2-layer with MLPs, not attention-only. All evidence is figure-only, with no numeric step locations for the bump.

versions.untested_parts: No direct head identification, circuit-composition measurement, or test of whether a previous-token head composes with another head to implement the skip-trigram mechanism.

The reported plots and descriptions do not establish that head formation, a sharp in-context-learning gain, and a loss bump occur at precisely the same point in a narrow early-training window; induction-head formation itself is not measured.
No large-transformer assessment of how much in-context learning is carried by induction heads, and no comparison of induction heads with other mechanisms for few-shot learning.
No survey of induction behavior across model families, sizes, or independent training runs. The RNN comparison concerns in-context loss, not induction-head behavior.
The study varies synthetic data structure and the number of ergodic components, but does not systematically measure whether or when induction heads form under those conditions.
The study does not distinguish few-shot task learning from repeated-token copying or measure which mechanisms carry few-shot task learning.
No analysis of induction-head formation as multiple sub-steps or overlapping transitions.
